paragraphs: Audio can be represented as a waveform or as features describing how its frequency content changes over time. The paper investigates generating audio through the second representation, focusing on the short-time Fourier transform. Although these features are useful for analyzing sound, generating features that can be converted back into satisfying audio presents additional challenges.

The authors examine the difficulties involved in synthesizing audio from generated, invertible time-frequency features and provide guidelines for addressing them. They then train a generative adversarial network on short-time Fourier features. This connects their discussion of representation choices to a working synthesis system, testing whether deliberate treatment of the feature domain can improve the resulting audio.

In the reported comparison, the feature-based network outperforms a state-of-the-art GAN that generates waveforms directly, even though the networks have similar architectures. The finding supports time-frequency modeling as a promising route for audio generation. It also shows why the representation and the way it is handled can matter alongside the network architecture.
icml-2019-adversarial-generation-of-time.tldr: Carefully designed generation of short-time Fourier features lets an audio GAN outperform a similarly structured waveform GAN in the reported comparison.

paragraphs: A data matrix can contain meaningful relationships among both its rows and its columns. Representation learning often concentrates on only one of these two directions. This paper develops co-manifold learning for incomplete matrices, seeking representations that reveal the geometry of both directions while using the connection between them.

The method has three stages. First, it solves a family of optimization problems to produce completed versions of the matrix at different levels of smoothness. It then combines information from those versions into a new multiscale measure of distance between rows and between columns. These distances implicitly couple the two directions, so their representations are informed by a shared collection of matrix estimates.

Finally, the method constructs row and column representations from the resulting distances. The authors report better visualization and clustering performance than competing approaches. The contribution is therefore more than filling empty entries: the completion process supplies information at several scales that helps uncover structure on both sides of the matrix.
icml-2019-co-manifold-learning-with-miss.tldr: Co-manifold learning uses multiscale matrix completion to jointly reveal row and column structure, improving visualization and clustering in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Reducing high-dimensional data to a small set of coordinates can expose broad structure, but those coordinates may leave the original measurements difficult to interpret. This paper asks how variation in each original feature relates to a learned low-dimensional representation, additional observed variables, and nonlinear interactions between the two.

The proposed Covariate Gaussian Process Latent Variable Model, or c-GPLVM, addresses this question through a structured decomposition of its kernel. Within the hybrid Gaussian process model, that structure allows feature-level variation to be broken down according to the different sources the authors want to study. The model therefore combines learning a compact representation with interpreting variability in the original feature space.

The authors demonstrate the approach on simulated examples and disease progression applications involving high-dimensional gene expression and additional phenotypes. In these settings, it extracts low-dimensional structure while providing a breakdown of feature variability unavailable in commonly used dimensionality reduction approaches. This makes the representation useful for examining how measured features relate to latent structure and external covariates.
icml-2019-decomposing-feature-level-vari.tldr: c-GPLVM combines dimensionality reduction with a decomposition of feature variation into latent, covariate, and nonlinear interaction components.

paragraphs: The paper broadens the idea of disentanglement in variational autoencoders into a framework called decomposition. It identifies two requirements: individual data encodings should overlap appropriately, and their aggregate distribution should match a desired structure expressed through the prior. Independence between latent variables becomes one possible structure among several.

This perspective also accommodates sparsity, clusters, independent subspaces, and hierarchical dependencies. The authors show that the main difference between the beta-VAE and the standard VAE concerns control of encoding overlap. With the usual isotropic Gaussian prior, the beta-VAE objective is unchanged by rotations of the latent representation, so the objective does not distinguish among those rotated arrangements.

The authors show that simple prior modifications that break this rotational invariance can improve disentanglement with little or no damage to reconstruction. They also demonstrate how other priors encourage other decompositions and introduce a training objective that controls both factors in a principled way. The contribution links representation structure to explicit choices about overlap and the prior.
icml-2019-disentangling-disentanglement-.tldr: A two-factor view of VAE representations explains how encoding overlap and prior structure can support disentanglement and richer latent organizations.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning estimates a distribution of values, giving an agent more information than a single expected value. The paper observes that this distribution reflects both uncertainty about model parameters and uncertainty intrinsic to outcomes. Its exploration method uses that distribution while seeking to suppress the influence of intrinsic uncertainty.

The method combines two components: a decaying schedule for suppressing intrinsic uncertainty and an exploration bonus computed from the upper quantiles of the learned distribution. Upper quantiles describe the high-value part of that distribution. Using them to construct a bonus connects exploration decisions to potentially favorable outcomes represented by the learner.

Across 49 Atari 2600 games, the authors report a 483% average gain in cumulative rewards over QR-DQN. In the CARLA driving simulator, they report reaching near-optimal safety rewards twice as fast as QR-DQN. These findings support the exploration strategy in the evaluated settings, showing that a learned value distribution can guide exploration as well as represent possible returns.
icml-2019-distributional-reinforcement-l.tldr: An exploration bonus based on upper value quantiles, combined with suppression of intrinsic uncertainty, improves reported Atari rewards and CARLA learning speed over QR-DQN.

paragraphs: Dynamical systems can vary across individuals, groups, and whole populations. This paper introduces a Bayesian inference framework that represents these distinct levels of variability while modeling nonlinear behavior over time. Its model class extends nonlinear mixed-effects dynamical systems, allowing a broader combination of structured dynamics and learned components.

The dynamics are specified by an ordinary differential equation, with both the equation and its numerical solver made differentiable. The equation can combine user-prescribed components with neural network components. Parameter inference is formulated as stochastic optimization of a block-conditional variational autoencoder, bringing inference and the dynamical model into one differentiable training process.

The framework supports interpretation of the underlying dynamics and prediction for previously unseen combinations of group components. The authors empirically validate it by predicting the behavior of bacteria engineered as biosensors. They also argue that amortized inference with stochastic optimization could scale to massive experimental data pipelines; that scalability is presented as a capability of the approach rather than as the reported biological experiment itself.
icml-2019-efficient-amortised-bayesian-i.tldr: A differentiable Bayesian framework combines hierarchical variability, prescribed dynamics, and neural components to model nonlinear systems and predict unseen group combinations.

paragraphs: Many fairness criteria can be expressed through independence, or conditional independence, between model outcomes and sensitive variables. This paper extends that approach to continuous variables using the Rényi maximum correlation coefficient. The aim is to measure relevant dependence without first forcing a continuous attribute into categories separated by thresholds.

The authors use Witsenhausen’s characterization of this coefficient to develop a differentiable implementation connected to f-divergences. Their learning penalty upper-bounds the correlation coefficient, providing a way to discourage dependence during training. Because the penalty can be estimated from mini-batches, the approach can be used when training deep neural networks.

Experiments show favorable comparisons with state-of-the-art methods for binary variables and demonstrate protection of continuous variables. The contribution broadens the variables that fairness-aware learning can directly handle, including financial status and representations of mixed ethnic groups. Its significance lies in combining a continuous dependence measure with a trainable penalty, making the fairness criterion part of the learning process.
icml-2019-fairness-aware-learning-for-co.tldr: A differentiable penalty based on Rényi maximum correlation extends fairness-aware learning to continuous sensitive variables without thresholding them into categories.

paragraphs: Some statistical estimates are entire functions or other complex objects rather than short vectors of numbers. This paper studies how Gaussian perturbations can provide differential privacy for estimates in separable Banach spaces, which may be infinite-dimensional. That setting allows the privacy analysis to address a broad range of functional data summaries.

The authors use classical probability results to show how densities over spaces of functions can establish the required privacy bounds. Their analysis extends earlier results to a wider collection of outputs, including path-level summaries, nonlinear functionals, and complete functions. The contribution brings these richer releases into a common mathematical treatment of Gaussian privacy mechanisms.

The paper also examines the role of regularization in balancing privacy and usefulness. An application to penalized smoothing illustrates that balance when estimating a mean function. Simulations and an application to diffusion tensor imaging provide additional demonstrations. Together, the theory and examples clarify how protecting complex statistical outputs depends on the structure of the estimates and their regularization.
icml-2019-formal-privacy-for-functional-.tldr: The paper extends Gaussian differential privacy analysis to function-valued estimates and examines how regularization balances privacy with statistical usefulness.

paragraphs: When predictions are distributions over classes, the classes may have meaningful distances or costs between them. This paper generalizes logistic loss so that those relationships become part of the learning objective. Its construction combines entropy-regularized optimal transport with a duality between measures and continuous functions.

The resulting loss gives unconstrained convex objective functions and supports class spaces that are extremely large or infinite. It also produces a geometric counterpart of the softmax operator. These properties connect the representation of predictions to the geometry of the possible outcomes, while retaining the stated convex structure of the proposed objectives.

The loss is suitable for predicting sparse or singular distributions, including distributions concentrated on curves or hypersurfaces. That matters when the desired output occupies a structured subset of the available space. The authors analyze the loss theoretically and demonstrate its effectiveness in ordinal regression and drawing generation, illustrating its use for both ordered outcomes and geometrically structured outputs.
icml-2019-geometric-losses-for-distribut.tldr: A geometric generalization of logistic loss incorporates distances between classes and supports structured distributions over very large or infinite output spaces.

paragraphs: Privacy mechanisms often release noisy measurements that summarize a data distribution. A subsequent task is to use those measurements to estimate answers to additional questions about the data. This paper focuses on making that estimation process efficient, using graphical models to organize the information available in the noisy summaries.

The approach is particularly effective when the data have many dimensions but each measurement concerns a low-dimensional marginal, meaning a distribution over a small subset of variables. This distinction is central to the problem: the full distribution may be large even though the released measurements each describe only a limited portion of it.

The authors show that their approach is substantially more efficient than existing estimation techniques from the privacy literature. They also show that it can improve the accuracy and scalability of many state-of-the-art privacy mechanisms. The contribution concerns how released measurements are used for inference, making graphical modeling a practical component of a broader private data-analysis process.
icml-2019-graphical-model-based-estimati.tldr: Graphical models make inference from noisy private measurements more efficient, especially for high-dimensional data summarized by low-dimensional marginals.

paragraphs: An observed event sequence may omit events that help explain what happened. Given a probability model of complete continuous-time sequences, this paper develops a method for inferring those missing events. It uses particle smoothing, which constructs multiple candidate complete sequences through sequential importance sampling.

The proposal distributions are trainable and use a bidirectional continuous-time LSTM. Bidirectionality allows proposed missing events to depend on later observations as well as earlier ones. This is the central difference from particle filtering: an event observed later in the sequence can help determine what may have been missing earlier.

From the sampled complete sequences, the method forms a consensus prediction with low Bayes risk under the authors’ chosen loss. Experiments cover synthetic and real domains with different missingness mechanisms, using a neural Hawkes process to model complete sequences. On held-out incomplete sequences, the method effectively infers unobserved events, and particle smoothing consistently improves on particle filtering in the reported experiments.
icml-2019-imputing-missing-events-in-con.tldr: Bidirectional particle smoothing uses earlier and later observations to infer missing continuous-time events, improving on particle filtering in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Compiler designers and performance engineers need estimates of how many processor cycles a block of assembly instructions takes in steady-state execution. Constructing analytical models for modern x86-64 processors is difficult because their internal behavior is sophisticated. Those hand-built models also require renewed effort for each processor generation.

Ithemal learns to predict this throughput from the instructions themselves. Its hierarchical LSTM-based model takes the opcodes and operands of a basic block as input. The approach makes learned prediction the central mechanism for estimating execution cost, reducing reliance on manually constructing a detailed analytical model for every target microarchitecture.

The authors report less than half the prediction error of LLVM’s llvm-mca and Intel’s IACA, while matching their prediction speed. They also report that Ithemal can be ported across several processor microarchitectures with little developer effort. These findings connect accuracy, runtime, and portability: the learned approach improves the reported estimates while remaining fast enough to compare favorably with established analysis tools.
icml-2019-ithemal-accurate-portable-and-.tldr: Ithemal learns assembly-block throughput with less than half the reported error of two analytical tools while matching their speed and easing portability.

paragraphs: MIWAE addresses training deep latent variable models when the training data contain missing values. The method assumes missing-at-random data and adapts the importance-weighted autoencoder to optimize a potentially tight lower bound on the likelihood of the observed entries. This lets the learning objective directly target the available evidence.

The authors state that handling missing data introduces no additional computational overhead relative to the original importance-weighted autoencoder. They also develop Monte Carlo procedures for filling in missing values after training. These support both single imputation, which produces one completion, and multiple imputation, which produces several possible completions from the learned model.

The paper demonstrates training a convolutional model on incomplete static binarizations of MNIST. On several continuous datasets, it reports highly accurate single imputations that are strongly competitive with state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines learning from incomplete data and completing that data within the same generative modeling framework, with the missing-at-random assumption defining the stated training setting.
icml-2019-miwae-deep-generative-modellin.tldr: MIWAE trains deep generative models on missing-at-random data and uses them for accurate single or multiple imputation without added missing-data training overhead.

paragraphs: This paper gives a complete mathematical characterization of the explicit regularization induced by dropout in deep linear networks trained with squared loss. The setting is specific: the results concern networks whose layers are linear and an objective based on squared prediction errors. Within that setting, the analysis identifies exactly how dropout modifies the optimization problem.

The induced penalty contains an l2 path regularizer together with additional terms that are invariant to rescaling. The authors also show that its convex envelope is the squared nuclear norm of the network’s overall map. A convex envelope is the largest convex function lying below the original penalty, so this result establishes a precise connection between dropout’s penalty and a matrix-level regularizer.

For a sufficiently large dropout rate, the paper further characterizes the global optima of the dropout objective. The authors support their theoretical findings with empirical results. Together, these contributions clarify both the form of the regularization and the solutions it produces under the stated dropout-rate condition.
icml-2019-on-dropout-and-nuclear-norm-re.tldr: For deep linear networks with squared loss, the paper characterizes dropout’s regularizer, its squared-nuclear-norm convex envelope, and global optima at sufficiently large dropout rates.

paragraphs: Invariant networks are designed to give the same output when an input undergoes specified symmetry transformations. This paper asks whether networks built from symmetry-respecting linear layers can approximate every continuous invariant function. It considers groups that act by permuting input coordinates, covering an arbitrary subgroup of the symmetric group.

The first main result establishes universality when the network is allowed to use higher-order tensors. The second shows that these richer representations are essential for some groups: restricting the network to first-order tensors can prevent universality. Thus, enforcing the desired symmetry alone does not settle whether an architecture has enough expressive power.

Because first-order representations are practically attractive, the authors also prove a necessary condition for universality in that restricted setting. They conjecture that the condition is sufficient as well, but do not present that sufficiency as a theorem. The paper therefore establishes both a general route to universality and a sharper boundary around what simpler invariant architectures can express.
icml-2019-on-the-universality-of-invaria.tldr: Permutation-invariant networks are universal with higher-order tensors, and some symmetry groups require those tensors to achieve universality.

paragraphs: Boosting builds a predictor by repeatedly adding base hypotheses to a linear combination. Its generalization error can continue improving after training error reaches zero, and increasing prediction margins is one proposed explanation. This paper studies how efficiently boosting can improve the smallest margin among all training examples.

The central trade-off is between that minimum margin and the number of base hypotheses trained. Earlier work had led to a conjecture that AdaBoostV achieved the optimal trade-off. The authors introduce a new algorithm that refutes the conjecture, showing that the previously proposed limit on this trade-off was not the correct one.

They also prove a lower bound that establishes the optimality of their new algorithm for the trade-off under study. The contribution therefore includes both an improved construction and a matching statement about what can be achieved. Its meaning is specific to minimum-margin maximization with a limited number of hypotheses, giving a precise resolution to that boosting question.
icml-2019-optimal-minimal-margin-maximiz.tldr: A new boosting algorithm disproves AdaBoostV’s conjectured optimality and achieves a hypothesis-count versus minimum-margin trade-off certified by a lower bound.

paragraphs: Learning-theory bounds often cover every classifier in a hypothesis class, including choices that do not optimize the learning objective. This paper instead analyzes the sample complexity of optimal kernel sum classifiers. The distinction makes optimality part of the statistical analysis, allowing the argument to use information about how the classifier was selected.

The authors combine optimization tools with learning-theory bounds to carry out this analysis. Their approach focuses on classifiers formed through kernel sums and uses their optimality to study statistical efficiency. This ties the optimization problem to the question of how much data learning requires, rather than treating the entire candidate class as an undifferentiated collection.

The analysis also justifies assumptions used in earlier work on multiple kernel learning. As a further result, the paper introduces a form of Rademacher complexity for hypothesis classes containing only optimal classifiers. That provides a complexity measure aligned with the paper’s central idea: statistical guarantees can account explicitly for the restriction to optimized solutions.
icml-2019-optimality-implies-kernel-sum-.tldr: Combining optimization and learning theory yields sample-complexity analysis and a Rademacher-complexity formulation specifically for optimal kernel sum classifiers.

paragraphs: In a configurable Markov decision process, learning can involve changing both the agent’s behavior and the environment’s configuration. The purpose of configuring the environment is to improve the agent’s performance. This paper addresses the lack of a suitable learning algorithm for applying that framework to real-world continuous domains.

The proposed method, Relative Entropy Model Policy Search, or REMPS, uses a trust-region approach to learn the policy and the configuration together. It does not require knowledge of the environment’s true model. This is central to its intended use: the learner can seek useful changes to the configurable environment without first being given its exact dynamics.

The authors provide a finite-sample analysis and evaluate REMPS in both benchmark and realistic environments, comparing it with gradient methods. The contribution connects the configurable decision-process formulation to an algorithm for continuous settings. Its analysis and evaluations examine joint learning of behavior and environment configuration as a concrete reinforcement-learning problem.
icml-2019-reinforcement-learning-in-conf.tldr: REMPS jointly learns a policy and environment configuration in continuous domains without requiring the environment’s true model.

paragraphs: Quantization helps make neural networks practical on embedded devices, but it can degrade their performance. This paper exploits a freedom in many networks: an output channel in one layer can be scaled if the corresponding weights in the next layer are scaled inversely. These coordinated changes preserve the network’s function.

That freedom produces multiple weight factorizations for the same underlying computation. The authors develop a simple method for choosing factorizations that reduce the damage introduced by quantization. The key observation is that functionally equivalent weight arrangements can behave differently once their numerical representation is quantized, making the factorization itself useful to optimize.

The authors report improvements across a wide variety of networks and state-of-the-art quantization degradation results for MobileNets. These findings show that changing the weight representation can improve quantization outcomes without changing the function before quantization. They also identify pruning, regularization, and interpretability as possible application areas for the factorization idea, while their reported focus is quantization.
icml-2019-same-same-but-different-recove.tldr: Function-preserving rescaling across neighboring layers reduces quantization degradation, with reported improvements across networks and state-of-the-art results for MobileNets.

paragraphs: The paper studies objectives that combine a smooth, nonconvex loss with a regularizer that is both nonsmooth and nonconvex. This combination makes the optimization problem different from one with a smooth loss alone. The authors focus on stochastic gradient methods for this setting, where finite-time convergence results had been relatively limited.

They introduce two simple algorithms covering finite-sum optimization and general stochastic optimization. In a finite-sum problem, the objective is assembled from a collection of terms; the general stochastic setting accommodates optimization through random information more broadly. Addressing both forms makes the contribution relevant to two distinct formulations of the regularized learning problem.

The main stated finding is improved convergence complexity compared with the current state of the art for this problem class. The authors also compare the algorithms empirically on empirical risk minimization. The theoretical contribution concerns how efficiently the methods meet their convergence criteria, while the practical comparisons examine their behavior when optimizing learning objectives.
icml-2019-simple-stochastic-gradient-met.tldr: Two stochastic gradient algorithms improve convergence complexity for smooth nonconvex losses combined with nonsmooth nonconvex regularizers.

paragraphs: Signed graphs contain positive relationships that attract nodes and negative relationships that repel them. This paper extends spectral clustering to handle both kinds of information through a family of Signed Power Mean Laplacians. A single parameter controls how matrix power means combine the normalized Laplacian structures associated with positive and negative edges.

The authors analyze this construction under a general stochastic block model that includes labeled and censored block models. They show that the expected signed power mean Laplacian captures the true clusters in certain reasonable settings where state-of-the-art approaches fail. They also prove concentration results for its eigenvalues and eigenvector under stated conditions in that model.

Those concentration results connect the behavior of random graphs to the behavior predicted by the expected matrix. Experiments on random graphs and real datasets confirm the theoretically predicted behavior and compare favorably with state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines a flexible treatment of attractive and repulsive relations with conditional theoretical support and empirical evidence.
icml-2019-spectral-clustering-of-signed-.tldr: Signed Power Mean Laplacians combine positive and negative graph relations, recovering cluster structure under analyzed conditions and performing favorably in experiments.

paragraphs: Stochastic blockmodels describe graphs through latent structure that can support community discovery and link prediction. Graph neural networks learn useful node representations by exploiting graph properties. This paper brings these approaches together in a sparse variational autoencoder, seeking the interpretability of blockmodels alongside the predictive strengths of graph neural networks.

The framework is developed for an overlapping stochastic blockmodel, allowing the latent community structure to reflect overlapping memberships. It includes a fast recognition model for inferring node embeddings. That inference component is useful within the combined system and is also relevant to inference in stochastic blockmodels and their variants.

On several benchmarks, the authors report encouraging link-prediction results while learning interpretable latent structure usable for community discovery. They also state that the framework can be readily adapted to other types of stochastic blockmodels. The contribution connects predictive embeddings with a generative account of graph structure, so the learned representation can serve both prediction and interpretation.
icml-2019-stochastic-blockmodels-meet-gr.tldr: A sparse graph variational autoencoder combines stochastic blockmodel interpretability with graph-neural-network prediction and fast node-embedding inference.

paragraphs: The Wasserstein transform is a method for enhancing and denoising datasets in general metric spaces. Its construction draws on optimal transportation ideas. Working in a metric space means the method is formulated around distances between data points, giving it a setting broader than datasets represented only by ordinary Euclidean coordinates.

The authors establish stability under data perturbations, addressing how the transform behaves when the input data change. For datasets assumed to be Euclidean, they also derive a precise connection to the mean shift family of algorithms. They use that connection to prove that mean shift inherits stability under perturbations as well.

The paper studies the transform as a preprocessing step before clustering and classification on different datasets. This places its enhancement and denoising role ahead of downstream analysis. The theoretical contribution is twofold: stability for the new transform and a route from its Euclidean connection to a stability result for mean shift, alongside the reported study of downstream use.
icml-2019-the-wasserstein-transform-54fd.tldr: The Wasserstein transform denoises metric-space data with proved stability and yields a stability result for mean shift through a Euclidean connection.

paragraphs: An advertising auction affects which audiences actually see an advertiser’s message. This paper proposes maximizing platform revenue subject to constraints on how that audience is distributed across sensitive types, such as gender or race. Fairness therefore enters the allocation mechanism itself through explicit restrictions on audience coverage.

Building on auction theory, the authors derive an optimal mechanism for a large class of fairness constraints. Choosing its parameters creates a nonconvex optimization problem. They reformulate it into a more structured nonconvex problem without saddle points or local maxima, and use that structure to develop a gradient-descent-based solution algorithm.

On the A1 Yahoo! dataset, the algorithm achieves uniform coverage across user types for each advertiser with a minor reduction in platform revenue and a small change in audience size. The finding demonstrates a favorable trade-off in the evaluated data. The theoretical optimality concerns the specified constrained auction problem, while the empirical result shows what enforcing those constraints can cost in practice.
icml-2019-toward-controlling-discriminat.tldr: A constrained ad auction achieves uniform audience coverage in the reported evaluation with minor revenue loss and small audience-size changes.

paragraphs: A learned optimizer is trained to improve another model, but training that optimizer can itself be unstable. The paper identifies a problem with truncated backpropagation through optimization: short unrolls produce strongly biased gradients, while long unrolls can produce exploding gradient norms. These difficulties obstruct learning useful optimization behavior.

The proposed training scheme dynamically weights two unbiased gradient estimators for a variational loss measuring optimizer performance. The authors show that this addresses both training difficulties and lets neural networks learn to optimize a specific task faster than tuned first-order methods. The objective used to train the optimizer also determines which aspects of performance it is encouraged to improve.

In particular, training against validation loss enables learned optimizers that produce better generalization than first-order methods. The authors demonstrate convolutional-network training problems with faster wall-clock optimization and improved test loss. These are task-specific empirical results, supporting the value of both the gradient-estimation scheme and the choice to optimize validation performance.
icml-2019-understanding-and-correcting-p.tldr: Dynamically combining unbiased gradient estimators enables learned optimizers that outperform tuned first-order methods in wall-clock time and test loss on demonstrated tasks.
